body:
Schnorg reported 2x increase in performance for these functions, presumably with a specific benchmark.

It did indeed seem faster in some situations for me when I tested, and no evidence of being slower in any (some benchmark scenes it made no significant difference for me).

It will depend how much these are a bottleneck in a particular game. But hey, free speedup! :+1: 

The other one he mentioned was that BVH doesn't take advantage of multiple threads for BVH heavy games. This was a deliberate decision at the time (there are some trade-offs here, and 3.x is primarily used single-threaded), but might be worth experimenting with for 4.x, I'll leave that to @Schnorg.

Yep, just finished my first round of testing my multithreading also (same benchmark, my horde game prototype with enemies all chasing player).

MacOS M5 10 core - Massive speed up ~3x
Windows 11 AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 8 core, 16 thread - Massive speed up ~3x
Linux Ubuntu NUC (12 years old, reporting 4 cores, think it is a low end Intel i5) - 20-30%
iOS 26.6, iPhone 11 Pro - 10 - 20% (pretty neglible)

The multithreading approach was not slower on any of my devices. I have more work to do though, just to make it all neat. I have a steam deck and iPad I might be able to test on also.

There is power consumption to consider, but I think that would be dominated by the GPU, and the CPU is already using worker threads for physics solving. For horde type games, the BVH has been the hot path. With the sign bit optimisation (and multithreading) the hot path seems to move to flush_queries (for this sort of test scenario).
